strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time control of diffusion-model alignment across reward preferences and KL regularization without retraining for every setting.
The core idea of blending reverse diffusion processes from separately fine-tuned models is simple, practical, and potentially useful for deployment when users need adjustable trade-offs.

The paper gives both a theoretical motivation and concrete algorithms, DB-MPA and DB-KLA, and compares against several relevant baselines including Rewarded Soup, reward-gradient guidance, CoDe, and an oracle-style MORL retraining baseline.

Experiments show consistent reward improvements over baselines on the reported settings, and the inference-time cost comparison helps clarify the practical trade-off relative to guidance/search methods.
Qualitative results suggest smooth controllability over reward weights and KL strength, which is a compelling property if it holds more broadly.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation appears fragile. In the reverse SDE, changing the score should introduce the diffusion/noise-schedule scaling and sign associated with the score term, but Proposition 1 states the added control as just the gradient of a log expectation. This seems inconsistent with the earlier SDE definition and undermines the claimed principled derivation unless clarified or corrected.

The key approximation relies on a Jensen-gap-style interchange of expectation and exponential, but the resulting error bound is hard to interpret or verify in practice and does not yield a clear condition under which DB-MPA/DB-KLA should work for real text-to-image diffusion models.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: the main train/test prompts are only 25 color prompts each, with a synthetic GPT-generated test set. This is not enough to establish broad multi-preference alignment for text-to-image generation.

Evaluation depends almost entirely on the same automated reward models used for optimization/control. There is no human preference study, no robust perceptual quality/diversity analysis, and no convincing check for reward hacking or distributional degradation.

The baseline comparison may be incomplete or under-tuned. Guidance methods are expensive but flexible, Rewarded Soup is a strong direct comparator, and the paper does not sufficiently explore sensitivity to hyperparameters, reward scaling, number of rewards, or model families.

DB-KLA results are mostly qualitative/figure-based in the main text, with limited quantitative reporting and no detailed analysis of actual KL divergence or distance from the base model despite KL control being a central claim.

Reproducibility is weakened by an apparently missing code URL in the abstract and by implementation details that are not sufficient to fully reproduce the RL fine-tuning and reward normalization choices.
The method has a real memory/computation cost because it runs multiple fine-tuned models at inference; the paper acknowledges this but does not deeply quantify scaling beyond small reward dimensions.

strengths: The paper targets an important and practical problem: controlling text-to-image diffusion alignment at inference time across multiple reward preferences and KL strengths without retraining for every setting.

The proposed method is simple and potentially useful: blending denoiser/backward-process outputs from separately RL-finetuned models is easy to implement and has a clear connection to model interpolation ideas.

The manuscript includes comparisons against several relevant baselines, including Rewarded Soup, reward-gradient guidance, CoDe, and an oracle-like MORL retraining baseline, plus some runtime measurements.
The paper attempts to provide theoretical motivation for why reward-mixture and KL-control blending might approximate the desired aligned diffusion process.
weaknesses: The empirical evaluation is much too narrow for the strength of the claims. Main results use only 25 test prompts, largely color/object prompts, with 25 related training prompts. This is not enough to support broad claims about inference-time multi-preference alignment for diffusion models.

The evaluation relies almost entirely on the same reward models used for optimization or closely related automatic reward proxies. There is no human preference study, no robust assessment of visual quality, diversity, prompt fidelity beyond the optimized reward, or reward hacking/failure analysis.

The theoretical contribution is weakly supported. The key approximation depends on Jensen-gap terms that are not empirically estimated or shown to be small in the actual Stable Diffusion setting, and the assumptions about conditional distributions/reward predictability are not convincingly justified for high-dimensional image generation and learned reward models.

The paper overclaims optimality and Pareto performance. MORL is described as an empirical upper bound, but it is just separately finetuned models under a particular training recipe and may not represent the true optimum. Claims such as 'theoretically maximum' are not justified.

Baselines may not be sufficiently tuned or fairly compared. CoDe and RGG are run only for a few weights due to cost, and the paper does not provide enough sensitivity analysis or hyperparameter tuning evidence to establish that the reported gaps are robust.

The method has substantial inference-time memory and compute costs because it requires running multiple denoisers/models. The paper reports higher latency than SD/RS but does not deeply analyze scaling with more rewards, deployment constraints, batching, or memory footprint.

DB-KLA extrapolates with coefficients such as lambda > 1, implying negative weight on the pretrained drift in the stated formula. The stability and validity of this extrapolation are not theoretically or empirically examined beyond small qualitative examples.

Reproducibility is limited: the abstract says code is available but the link appears blank, and many implementation details needed to reproduce RL finetuning, reward normalization, checkpoint selection, and baseline tuning are insufficiently specified.

The writing contains several errors and imprecisions, including typos, inconsistent naming, and at least one apparent equation typo in the proof of Proposition 1. These issues further reduce confidence in technical care.
Overall, while the idea is plausible and the early results are interesting, the paper does not yet provide the breadth, rigor, or reproducibility expected for acceptance at a top-tier AI conference.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and practical problem: inference-time control over multiple alignment rewards and KL regularization for diffusion models without retraining for each preference setting.

The proposed Diffusion Blend idea is conceptually clean: blend reverse diffusion/drift processes from basis RL-finetuned models, yielding simple algorithms for both multi-reward preference control (DB-MPA) and KL-strength control (DB-KLA).

The theoretical development provides a useful first-principles connection between reward-tilted target distributions and modified reverse diffusion dynamics, and the Jensen-gap approximation gives some justification for linear blending.

The empirical results are encouraging: DB-MPA consistently improves over Rewarded Soup, reward-gradient guidance, and CoDe on the reported metrics, and often approaches the per-preference MORL retraining oracle.

The paper evaluates both reward-combination control and KL-control, includes qualitative and quantitative results, reports inference-time comparisons, and provides appendices with prompts, hyperparameters, and additional results.
weaknesses: The experimental setting is quite narrow for a top-tier claim: the main evaluation uses SDv1.5, a small set of 25 train and 25 test prompts mostly focused on color/object compositional prompts, and only a few reward dimensions. It is unclear whether the method generalizes to richer prompts, styles, safety objectives, or modern diffusion backbones.

Evaluation relies heavily on the same learned reward models used for optimization, with no human preference study and limited assessment of visual quality, diversity, artifacts, reward hacking, or distributional degradation. This weakens the evidence that higher reward scores correspond to genuinely better alignment.

The theoretical approximation is plausible but not fully validated. The Jensen-gap error terms depend on assumptions that may fail for complex rewards or high-noise timesteps, and the paper does not empirically measure approximation error or characterize when blending breaks down.

The method has nontrivial deployment costs: DB-MPA requires running or storing multiple finetuned models at inference time, and inference time grows with the number of basis rewards. The memory and latency implications are acknowledged but not deeply addressed.

The comparison to baselines is useful but incomplete. Rewarded Soup is a strong relevant baseline, but more recent controllable/conditional finetuning methods, adapter-merging variants, or distillation-based alternatives are not thoroughly explored. Some baselines also appear tuned under different computational tradeoffs.

Reproducibility is only partial: hyperparameters and prompts are listed, but the abstract says code is available without an actual visible link, and implementation details for applying drift blending to practical latent diffusion samplers could be clearer.

The paper sometimes overstates the strength of the result, e.g. suggesting Pareto-optimal or near-oracle behavior, despite evidence being limited to small-scale empirical settings and approximate reward-model metrics.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: inference-time control of multi-objective reward alignment and KL strength for diffusion models without retraining for each preference setting.
The core idea of blending reverse diffusion drifts from separately reward-aligned models is simple, practically useful, and well motivated by the KL-regularized alignment formulation.

The paper provides a reasonably broad empirical study across SD v1.5, GenEval-style prompts, multiple reward models, conflicting rewards, more than two rewards, KL-control experiments, and an SDXL single-prompt extension.

Baselines are mostly appropriate, including parameter interpolation, reward-gradient guidance, gradient-free search, and separately fine-tuned oracle models. The reported inference-time comparison is useful, especially for the low-cost DB-MPA-LS variant.
The method appears practically attractive: DB-MPA-LS gives near base-model inference cost while retaining much of the benefit of drift blending.
weaknesses: The main theoretical justification relies on a Jensen-style approximation whose error terms are difficult to evaluate and are not empirically validated. It is unclear when the approximation is accurate for real text-to-image reward models and latent diffusion samplers.

The DB-MPA-LS continuous-time proposition is mathematically questionable as stated: an independently resampled Bernoulli variable at every continuous time is not a standard well-defined stochastic process, and the practical discretized sampler may not exactly inherit the claimed marginal equivalence.

Evaluation relies heavily on the same learned reward models used for optimization. There is no human preference study, little assessment of reward hacking, and limited reporting of image fidelity, diversity, or distributional degradation beyond reward scores and selected qualitative examples.

The strongest experiments use a small color-focused DrawBench subset for training, with GPT-generated evaluation prompts that remain close to the training distribution. This limits evidence for broad real-world prompt generalization.

The MORL baseline is repeatedly described as a theoretical optimum or oracle, but in practice it is only an empirical separately fine-tuned model and can itself underfit or fail; this somewhat overstates the comparison.

Several implementation details needed for reproducibility are deferred to code or remain underspecified, including exact LoRA/model checkpoints, reward normalization choices, random seeds, and how drift blending maps onto practical latent diffusion parameterizations and schedulers.

The paper would be stronger with ablations on reward scaling, number and diversity of basis rewards, negative or out-of-simplex weights, robustness to poorly trained basis models, and direct comparisons against conditional multi-reward fine-tuning approaches.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: inference-time control over multiple reward preferences and KL strength for diffusion-model alignment without retraining for every preference setting.
The proposed drift/score blending idea is simple and potentially useful in practice, especially when only a small number of reward-specific LoRA adapters are available.
The experiments include several baselines, multiple reward models, an efficient sampling variant, and some stress tests such as conflicting rewards and more than two objectives.
weaknesses: The core technical justification rests on strong approximations that are not empirically validated. The Jensen-gap approximation is central to the method, but the paper does not measure the approximation error or explain when it is small for real latent diffusion models, LoRA fine-tuning, classifier-free guidance, or practical DDIM-style samplers.

Several theoretical claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly suggests Pareto-optimal or oracle-like behavior, but the derivation only gives an approximate linearity statement under restrictive assumptions, and the MORL baseline is a finite retraining reference rather than a true maximum achievable performance.

The evaluation is largely circular: the same automated reward models used for training are used as the main evaluation metrics. There is no human preference study, no independent perceptual quality metric, no diversity analysis, and limited use of task-grounded metrics despite claims about semantic alignment and image quality.

The empirical setup is narrow. The main SD1.5 training uses only 25 DrawBench color prompts, with GPT-generated similar test prompts. The SDXL evidence is only a single-prompt experiment, which is far too weak to support scalability claims.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. RGG is modified with gradient normalization, CoDe and RGG are evaluated on fewer weights due to cost, baseline tuning details are sparse, and it is unclear whether each baseline received comparable hyperparameter effort. This weakens the main superiority claims.

DB-MPA-LS is theoretically fragile: the continuous-time random-drift proposition does not directly justify discrete adapter sampling in practical diffusion samplers, and the paper gives little analysis of variance, seed sensitivity, or cases where stochastic adapter selection degrades outputs.

Important practical costs are understated. DB-MPA requires storing and evaluating one fine-tuned model per basis reward, and the paper does not adequately analyze memory, batching constraints, or behavior as the number of objectives grows beyond the small tested cases.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Key prompt lists are deferred to code, the paper lacks confidence intervals or statistical tests, and training details are insufficient to assess whether the reported gains are robust across seeds, checkpoints, and reward-model calibration choices.

The writing contains avoidable errors and imprecision, including typos in mathematical statements, inconsistent naming, and strong language such as 'maximum achievable' and 'extensive' that is not matched by the evidence.

The impact statement is too dismissive for a method that makes reward optimization and preference steering easier in image generation; risks such as reward hacking, unsafe preference directions, and misuse of controllable generation are not meaningfully discussed.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: inference-time control over multiple reward preferences and KL regularization for diffusion-model alignment without retraining for each user-specified trade-off.

The core idea of blending reverse diffusion processes from reward-specific fine-tuned models is simple, intuitive, and useful, with clear algorithms for multi-preference alignment, KL control, and a lower-cost LoRA-sampling variant.
The paper provides a reasonably developed theoretical motivation connecting KL-regularized target distributions, reverse SDE drift shifts, and approximate linearity under a Jensen-gap approximation.

Empirical results are broad relative to many papers in this area: comparisons include Rewarded Soup, CoDe, reward-gradient guidance, and MORL oracle-style retraining; evaluations cover DrawBench-style prompts, GenEval, conflicting rewards, three/four reward settings, KL sweeps, and an SDXL sanity check.
DB-MPA-LS is a practically appealing contribution: it largely preserves DB-MPA performance while reducing inference cost close to the base diffusion model, which materially improves deployability.
The results are consistently favorable and the method appears to provide smooth, interpretable control over reward trade-offs and alignment strength.
weaknesses: The theoretical guarantees rely on strong approximations whose empirical validity is not directly measured. The Jensen-gap error terms are bounded but not estimated in experiments, so it is unclear when the approximation is expected to hold or fail in realistic high-dimensional diffusion settings.

The proof and statement of the LoRA-sampling/SDE equivalence are somewhat idealized. The use of an independently resampled Bernoulli variable at each continuous time is mathematically delicate, and the result does not fully justify the discretized sampler used in practice with finite denoising steps and neural-network parameterization.

The evaluation is strong in trends but still somewhat narrow in deployment realism. Much of the main evidence uses SD v1.5, small training prompt subsets, synthetic/LLM-generated test prompts, and reward-model metrics that may favor methods optimized for those same rewards.
The SDXL experiment is limited to a single prompt, so it supports feasibility rather than demonstrating scalability to modern large text-to-image models in a convincing way.

The paper would benefit from stronger ablations: sensitivity to KL weight alpha, number and diversity of fine-tuned basis models, negative or out-of-simplex weights, reward scale normalization, LoRA rank, sampler choice, and number of denoising steps are not explored deeply enough.

The baselines are reasonable, but some comparisons may be uneven because DB methods use trained reward-specific models while several guidance baselines are training-free or very expensive at inference. A more detailed compute-budget-normalized comparison would clarify the practical trade-offs.

Human evaluation is missing. Since reward models can be imperfect and reward hacking is a central concern, user studies or blind human preference comparisons would significantly strengthen the claims about visual quality and preference alignment.

Some presentation issues reduce confidence: there are typos and minor mathematical slips, and several important implementation details are deferred to code rather than being fully specified in the paper.
